paragraphs: Democratic People Can Have No Aptitude and No Taste for Science, Literature, or Art

It must be acknowledged that few of the civilized nations of our time have made less progress in the higher sciences than the United States, and few have produced fewer great artists, fine poets, or celebrated writers. Many Europeans, struck by this fact, have seen it as a natural and inevitable result of equality. They have supposed that if a democratic state of society and democratic institutions ever came to prevail over the whole earth, the human mind would gradually see its guiding lights grow dim, and people would fall back into an age of darkness. To reason this way is, I think, to confuse several ideas that it is important to separate and examine one by one. It is to mix together, without intending to, what is democratic with what is merely American.

The religion professed by the first emigrants and handed down by them to their descendants is simple in its worship, austere and almost harsh in its principles, and hostile to outward symbols and ceremonial pomp. It is naturally unfavorable to the fine arts, and it only grudgingly tolerates the pleasures of literature. The Americans are a very old and very educated people who have come upon a new and boundless country, where they can spread out as they please and which they can make fertile without difficulty. This situation has no parallel in the history of the world. In America, then, everyone finds opportunities, unknown elsewhere, to make or increase a fortune. The spirit of gain is always strained to the utmost, and the human mind, constantly drawn away from the pleasures of the imagination and the labors of the intellect, is moved there by no impulse but the pursuit of wealth. The United States has its manufacturing and commercial classes, as every other country does. But what has never happened elsewhere is that the whole community is engaged at once in productive industry and commerce. I am convinced that if the Americans had been alone in the world, with the freedom and knowledge their forefathers acquired and the passions that are their own, they would not have been slow to discover that progress in the application of the sciences cannot long continue without cultivating the theory behind them, and that all the arts are perfected by one another. However absorbed they might have been in pursuing the main object of their desires, they would soon have admitted that they must turn aside from it now and then, in order to reach it better in the end.

The taste for the pleasures of the mind is, moreover, so natural to the heart of civilized man that even among refined nations least inclined to give themselves up to such pursuits, a certain number of citizens are always found who take part in them. Once felt, this intellectual craving would very soon have been satisfied. But at the very time when the Americans were naturally inclined to ask nothing of science except its specific applications to the useful arts and the means of making life comfortable, learned and literary Europe was exploring the common sources of truth and, at the same time, improving everything that can serve the pleasures or meet the needs of man. Among the educated nations of the Old World, the inhabitants of the United States singled out one in particular, to which they were closely tied by a common origin and by kindred habits. Among this people they found distinguished men of science, skilled artists, and eminent writers, and they were able to enjoy the treasures of the intellect without having to labor to gather them. I cannot agree to separate America from Europe, in spite of the ocean between them. I regard the people of the United States as the part of the English people that has been given the task of exploring the wilds of the New World, while the rest of the nation, with more leisure and less worn down by the drudgery of life, can devote its energies to thought and extend the empire of the mind in every direction. The position of the Americans is therefore quite exceptional, and it may be believed that no democratic people will ever be placed in a similar one. Their strictly Puritan origin, their exclusively commercial habits, even the country they inhabit, which seems to draw their minds away from science, literature, and the arts, and the nearness of Europe, which lets them neglect these pursuits without falling back into barbarism, along with a thousand particular causes of which I have been able to point out only the most important, have all come together to fix the American’s mind on purely practical objects. His passions, his needs, his education, and everything around him seem to join in pulling the native of the United States toward the earth. His religion alone bids him turn, from time to time, a brief and distracted glance toward heaven. Let us stop, then, viewing all democratic nations through the mask of the American people, and let us try at last to look at them with their own proper features.

It is possible to imagine a people not divided into any castes or scale of ranks, in which the law recognizes no privileges and divides inherited property into equal shares, but which at the same time lacks both knowledge and freedom. Nor is this an empty hypothesis. A despot may find it in his interest to make his subjects equal and to leave them ignorant, so as to keep them more easily enslaved. A democratic people of this kind would show neither aptitude nor taste for science, literature, or art, and it would probably never come to possess them. The law of descent would by itself destroy fortunes in each succeeding generation, and no one would acquire new ones. The poor man, with neither knowledge nor freedom, would not even conceive the idea of raising himself to wealth, and the rich man would let himself be reduced to poverty without any thought of defending himself. Between these two members of the community a complete and unshakable equality would soon be established.

No one would then have the time or the taste to devote himself to the pursuits or pleasures of the intellect. All men would remain paralyzed in a state of common ignorance and equal servitude. When I picture a democratic society of this kind, I imagine myself in one of those low, close, gloomy dwellings where the light that breaks in from outside soon grows faint and fades away. A sudden heaviness overcomes me, and I grope through the surrounding darkness to find the opening that will bring me back to daylight and fresh air.

But none of this applies to men who are already educated and who keep their freedom after abolishing among themselves those particular, hereditary rights that kept property permanently in the hands of certain individuals or certain bodies. When men living in a democratic state of society are educated, they readily see that no limits confine them or force them to put up with their present fortune. They therefore all conceive the idea of increasing it. If they are free, they all try, but they do not all succeed in the same way. The legislature, it is true, no longer grants privileges, but nature bestows them. Since natural inequality is very great, fortunes become unequal as soon as every man uses all his faculties to get rich. The law of descent prevents the establishment of wealthy families, but it does not prevent the existence of wealthy individuals. It constantly brings the members of the community back to a common level, and they constantly escape from it. The inequality of fortunes grows in proportion as knowledge spreads and liberty increases.

A sect that arose in our time, famous for its talents and its extravagance, proposed to concentrate all property in the hands of a central power, whose job it would then be to parcel it out to individuals according to their capacity. This would have been a way of escaping the complete and eternal equality that seems to threaten democratic society. But it would be a simpler and less dangerous remedy to grant no privilege to anyone, giving all people equal education and equal independence, and leaving each to determine his own position. Natural inequality will very soon make its own way, and wealth will pass of itself into the hands of the most capable.

Free and democratic communities, then, will always contain a considerable number of people who enjoy wealth or a comfortable competence. These wealthy people will not be as closely linked to one another as the members of the old aristocratic class were. Their tendencies will be different, and they will scarcely ever enjoy leisure that is as secure or as complete. But they will be far more numerous than the members of that class could ever be. These people will not be strictly confined to the cares of practical life, and they will still be able, though in different degrees, to indulge in the pursuits and pleasures of the intellect. And they will indulge in them. For if it is true that the human mind leans on one side toward the narrow, the practical, and the useful, it naturally rises on the other side toward the infinite, the spiritual, and the beautiful. Physical needs tie it to the earth, but as soon as the tie is loosened, it will relax and rise again.

Not only will the number of people who can take an interest in the products of the mind grow, but the taste for intellectual enjoyment will spread, step by step, even to those who in aristocratic societies seem to have neither the time nor the ability to indulge in it. When hereditary wealth, the privileges of rank, and the prerogatives of birth have ceased to exist, and when every man draws his strength from himself alone, it becomes evident that the chief cause of the differences between men’s fortunes is the mind. Whatever tends to strengthen, extend, or adorn the mind instantly becomes very valuable. The usefulness of knowledge becomes strikingly obvious even to the multitude. Those who have no taste for its charms still value its results and make some effort to acquire it. In free and educated democratic ages, nothing separates men from one another or keeps them in their own particular sphere. They rise and fall with extreme rapidity. All classes live in constant contact because they are so close together. They talk and mingle every day, and they imitate and envy one another. This suggests to the people many ideas, notions, and desires that they would never have had if the distinctions of rank had been fixed and society at rest. In such nations the servant never regards himself as a complete stranger to the pleasures and toils of his master, nor the poor man to those of the rich. The rural population grows to resemble that of the towns, and the provinces that of the capital. No one easily lets himself be reduced to the merely material cares of life, and the humblest artisan now and then casts an eager, furtive glance into the higher regions of the intellect. People do not read with the same ideas or in the same way as in an aristocratic community, but the circle of readers keeps widening until it includes all the citizens.

As soon as the multitude begins to take an interest in the labors of the mind, it finds that excelling in some of them is a powerful way to gain fame, power, or wealth. The restless ambition that equality produces at once takes this direction, as it does every other. The number of people who cultivate science, letters, and the arts becomes immense. The intellectual world springs into prodigious activity. Everyone tries to open a path there for himself and to draw the eyes of the public after him. Something similar happens here to what happens in the political society of the United States. What is done is often imperfect, but the attempts are countless. And although the results of individual effort are usually very small, the total is always very large.

It is therefore not true to claim that men living in democratic ages are naturally indifferent to science, literature, and the arts. It must only be admitted that they cultivate them in their own way, and bring to the task their own particular strengths and weaknesses.
